*Translator's note:* That is, to Christ.

*Translator's note:* Or “chaste.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “I fear lest somehow.”

*Translator's note:* Or “the snake.”

*Translator's note:* Or “craftiness.”

*Translator's note:* Or “corrupted,” “seduced.”

*Text-critical note:* Although most mss (א2 H Ψ 0121 0243 1739 1881 M) lack “and pure” (καὶ τῆς ἁγνότητος, kai tēs hagnotētos; *Grk* “and purity”) several significant and early witnesses (P46 א* B D[2] F G 33 81 104 ar r co) retain these words. Their presence in such mss across such a wide geographical distribution argues for their authenticity. The omission from the majority of mss can be explained by haplography, since the -τητος ending of ἁγνότητος is identical to the ending of ἁπλότητος (haplotētos, “sincerity”) three words back (ἁπλότητος καὶ τῆς ἁγνότητος); further, since the meanings of “sincerity” and “purity” are similar they might seem redundant. A copyist would scarcely notice the omission because Paul’s statement still makes sense without “and from purity.”

*Translator's note:* Or “preaches.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “another Jesus whom we have not proclaimed.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “a different spirit which you did not receive.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “a different gospel which you did not accept.”

*Translator's note:* Or “you endure it very well.”

*Translator's note:* The implicit irony in Paul’s remark is brought out well by the TEV “I do not think that I am the least bit inferior to those very special so-called ‘apostles’ of yours!”

*Study note:* The ‘*super-apostles*’ refers either (1) to the original apostles (the older interpretation) or (2) more probably, to Paul’s opponents in Corinth, in which case the designation is ironic.
*Study note:* *Unskilled in speaking* means not professionally trained as a rhetorician.

*Study note:* Paul is referring to *humbling* himself to the point of doing manual labor to support himself.

*Translator's note:* Or “preached.”
*Study note:* That is, *serve* them free of charge (cf. the end of v. 7).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “you, and when.” A new sentence was started here in the translation.

*Translator's note:* If the participle ἐλθόντες (elthontes) is taken as temporal rather than adjectival, the translation would be, “for the brothers, when they came from Macedonia, fully supplied my needs” (similar to NASB).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “needs, and I kept.” A new sentence was started here in the translation.

*Translator's note:* That is, that Paul offers the gospel free of charge to the Corinthians (see 2 Cor 11:7).

*Translator's note:* Or “silenced.”
*Translator's note:* *Grk* “God knows!” The words “I do” are supplied for clarity. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context.
*Translator's note:* *Grk* “an opportunity, so that they may be found just like us.”

*Translator's note:* Or “also masquerade.”

*Translator's note:* Or “their works.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “with this confidence of boasting.” The genitive καυχήσεως (kauchēseōs) has been translated as an attributive genitive (the noun in the genitive functions as an adjective of the noun modified).

*Translator's note:* Or “say with the Lord’s authority.”

*Study note:* *Many* is a reference to Paul’s opponents.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “according to the flesh.”

*Translator's note:* Or “you tolerate.”

*Translator's note:* See L&N 88.212.

*Translator's note:* Or “my shame.”

*Study note:* It seems best, in context, to see the statement *we were too weak for that* as a parenthetical and ironic comment by Paul on his physical condition (weakness or sickness) while he was with the Corinthians (cf. 2 Cor 12:7-10; Gal 4:15).

*Translator's note:* The words “to boast about” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, and this phrase serves as the direct object of the preceding verb.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “I also dare”; the words “to boast about the same thing” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, and this phrase serves as the direct object of the preceding verb.
*Translator's note:* *Grk* “forty less one”; this was a standard sentence. “Lashes” is supplied to clarify for the modern reader what is meant.

*Study note:* *Beaten with a rod* refers to the Roman punishment of *admonitio* according to BDAG 902 s.v. ῥαβδίζω. {{Acts 16:22|Acts 16:22}} describes one of these occasions in Philippi; in this case it was administered by the city magistrates, who had wide powers in a military colony.

*Study note:* *Received a stoning*. See {{Acts 14:19|Acts 14:19}}, where this incident is described.

*Translator's note:* Or “bandits.” The word normally refers more to highwaymen (“robbers”) but can also refer to insurrectionists or revolutionaries (“bandits”).

*Translator's note:* Or “desert.”

*Translator's note:* The two different words for labor are translated “in hard work and toil” by L&N 42.48.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “in cold and nakedness.” Paul does not mean complete nakedness, however, which would have been repugnant to a Jew; he refers instead to the lack of sufficient clothing, especially in cold weather. A related word is used to 1 Cor 4:11, also in combination with experiencing hunger and thirst.

*Study note:* *Apart from other things*. Paul refers here either (1) to the external sufferings just mentioned, or (2) he refers to other things he has left unmentioned.

*Translator's note:* “Anxious concern,” so translated in L&N 25.224.
*Translator's note:* Or “who is caused to stumble.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “If boasting is necessary.”

*Translator's note:* Or “about the things related to my weakness.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “ethnarch.”

*Study note:* The *governor* was an official called an “ethnarch” who was appointed to rule on behalf of a king over a certain region.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “the city of the Damascenes.”

*Translator's note:* Or “to seize,” “to catch.”

*Translator's note:* In {{Acts 9:25|Acts 9:25}} the same basket used in Paul’s escape is called a σπυρίς (spuris), a basket larger than a κόφινος (kophinos). It was very likely made out of rope, so the translation “rope-basket” is used.

*Study note:* In the NT, *paradise* is mentioned three times. In Luke 23:43 it refers to the abode of the righteous dead. In Rev 2:7 it refers to the restoration of Edenic paradise predicted in {{Isaiah 51:3|Isa 51:3}} and {{Ezekiel 36:35|Ezek 36:35}}. The reference here in 2 Cor 12:4 is probably to be translated as parallel to the mention of the “third heaven” in v. 2. Assuming that the “first heaven” would be atmospheric heaven (the sky) and “second heaven” the more distant stars and planets, “third heaven” would refer to the place where God dwells. This is much more likely than some variation on the seven heavens mentioned in the pseudepigraphic book *2 Enoch* and in other nonbiblical and rabbinic works.

*Translator's note:* Or “things that cannot be put into words.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “a man.”

*Translator's note:* Or “speaking.”

*Translator's note:* Or “may think of.”

*Text-critical note:* Most mss (P46 D Ψ 1881 M) lack διό (dio, “Therefore”), but the widespread distribution and quality of mss which include it (א A B F G 0243 33 81 1175 1739) argues for its authenticity. Internally, its case is equally strong in that its inclusion is grammatically rough (διό is hardly necessary to convey purpose, especially since Paul uses ἵνα [hina, “so that”] next).

*Translator's note:* Or “to harass.”

*Translator's note:* The phrase “so that I might not become arrogant” is repeated here because it occurs in the Greek text two times in the verse. Although redundant, it is repeated because of the emphatic nature of its affirmation.

*Translator's note:* Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” because of the contrast implicit in the context.

*Translator's note:* Or “is sufficient.”

*Text-critical note:* The majority of later mss (א2 Ac D1 Ψ 0243 0278 33 1739 1881 M) as well as some versional witnesses include the pronoun “my” here, but the omission of the pronoun has excellent external support (P46vid א* A* B D* F G latt). Scribes probably added the pronoun for clarity, making the obvious referent explicit. This would also make “power” more parallel with “my grace.” Though the original text probably did not include “my,” scribes who added the word were following the sense of Paul’s statement.

*Translator's note:* The pronoun “my” was supplied in the translation to clarify the sense of Paul’s expression.

*Translator's note:* Or “my power comes to full strength.”

*Translator's note:* “Most gladly,” a comparative form used with superlative meaning and translated as such.

*Translator's note:* Or “may rest on.”

*Translator's note:* Or “I take delight in.”

*Translator's note:* Or “calamities.”
*Translator's note:* Or “I am in no way inferior.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “children ought not,” but this might give the impression that children are not supposed to support sick or aging parents in need of help. That is not what Paul is saying. His point is that children should not have to pay their parent’s way.
*Translator's note:* The Greek construction anticipates a negative answer, indicated by the ‘tag’ question “have I?” at the end of the clause. The question is rhetorical.

*Translator's note:* The words “to visit you” are not in the Greek text but are implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, and must be supplied for the modern reader.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “the.”

*Translator's note:* The Greek construction anticipates a negative answer, indicated by the ‘tag’ question “did he?” at the end of the clause.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “[Did we not walk] in the same tracks?” This is an idiom that means to imitate someone else or to behave as they do. Paul’s point is that he and Titus have conducted themselves in the same way toward the Corinthians. If Titus did not take advantage of the Corinthians, then neither did Paul.

*Text-critical note:* The reading “all this time” (πάλαι, palai) is found in several early and significant Alexandrian and Western witnesses including א* A B F G 0243 6 33 81 365 1175 1739 1881 lat; the reading πάλιν (palin, “again”) is read by א2 D Ψ 0278 M sy bo; the reading οὐ πάλαι (ou palai) is read by P46, making the question even more emphatic. The reading of P46 could only have arisen from πάλαι. The reading πάλιν is significantly easier (“are you once again thinking that we are defending ourselves?”), for it softens Paul’s tone considerably. It thus seems to be a motivated reading and cannot easily explain the rise of πάλαι. Further, πάλαι has considerable support in the Alexandrian and Western witnesses, rendering it virtually certain as the autographic wording here.

*Translator's note:* Or “for your strengthening”; *Grk* “for your edification.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and I will be found by you.” The passive construction has been converted to an active one in the translation.

*Translator's note:* The words “I am afraid that” are not repeated in the Greek text, but are needed for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “intense anger, hostility.”

*Translator's note:* The words “I am afraid that” are not repeated in the Greek text from v. 20, but are needed for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “I will mourn over.”

*Translator's note:* The word “visit” is not in the Greek text, but is implied.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “By the mouth.”

*Study note:* A quotation from {{Deuteronomy 19:15|Deut 19:15}} (also quoted in {{Matthew 18:16|Matt 18:16}}; 1 Tim 5:19).
*Translator's note:* The word “anyone” is not in the Greek text but is implied.
*Translator's note:* *Grk* “who.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation.
*Translator's note:* Or “unless indeed you are disqualified.”
*Translator's note:* Or “that we are not disqualified.”

*Translator's note:* Or “that we may appear to be approved.”

*Translator's note:* Or “what is good.”

*Translator's note:* Or “even if we appear disapproved.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “when I am present,” but in the context of Paul’s third (upcoming) visit to Corinth, this is better translated as “when I arrive.”

*Translator's note:* The words “with you” are not in the Greek text, but are implied.
*Translator's note:* *Grk* “brothers.” See note on the phrase “brothers and sisters” in 1:8.

*Study note:* The versification of vv. 12 and 13 in the NET (so also NRSV, NLT) is according to the versification in the NA28 and UBS5 editions of the Greek text. Some translations, however, break the material up into three verses, i.e., 12-14 (NKJV, NASB, NIV). The same material has been translated in each case; the only difference is the versification of that material.

*Translator's note:* Or “communion.”

*Text-critical note:* Most witnesses, especially later ones (א2 D Ψ M lat sy bo), conclude this letter with ἀμήν (amēn, “amen”), while several early and significant mss (P46 א* A B F G 0243 6 33 630 1175 1739 1881 sa) lack the particle. Such a conclusion is routinely added by scribes to NT books because a few of these books originally had such an ending (cf. Rom 16:27; Gal 6:18; {{Judges 25|Jude 25}}). A majority of Greek witnesses have the concluding ἀμήν in every NT book except Acts, James, and 3 John (and even in these books, ἀμήν is found in some witnesses). It is thus a predictable variant. That so many diverse witnesses lacked the word here is strong testimony to its absence for the original text of 2 Corinthians.
